# Book III, Proposition 35

*The rectangles contained by the segments are equal*

[Euclid's proof](#euclids-proof) · [In Lean](#in-lean) · [What it rests on](#what-it-rests-on) · [Mishnah](#mishnah)

> If in a circle two straight lines cut one another, the rectangle contained by the segments of the one is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments of the other.

**In Lean:** ✅ proved, as Euclid states it · Euclid's argument

<p align="center"><em>Cross AC and BD at E in a circle (red, blue): the rectangle contained by AE, EC equals the rectangle contained by DE, EB (both yellow).</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/III/35.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition III.35, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

For in the circle ABCD let the two straight lines AC, BD cut one another at the point E;

I say that the rectangle contained by AE, EC is equal to the rectangle contained by DE, EB.

If now AC, BD are through the centre, so that E is the centre of the circle ABCD,

it is manifest that, AE, EC, DE, EB being equal,

the rectangle contained by AE, EC is also equal to the rectangle contained by DE, EB.

Next let AC, DB not be through the centre;

let the centre of ABCD be taken, and let it be F;

from F let FG, FH be drawn perpendicular to the straight lines AC, DB, and let FB, FC, FE be joined.

Then, since a straight line GF through the centre cuts a straight line AC not through the centre at right angles,

it also bisects it; [III. 3]

therefore AG is equal to GC.

Since, then, the straight line AC has been cut into equal parts at G and into unequal parts at E,

the rectangle contained by AE, EC together with the square on EG is equal to the square on GC; [II. 5]

Let the square on GF be added;

therefore the rectangle AE, EC together with the squares on GE, GF is equal to the squares on CG, GF.

But the square on FE is equal to the squares on EG, GF,

and the square on FC is equal to the squares on CG, GF; [I. 47]

therefore the rectangle AE, EC together with the square on FE is equal to the square on FC.

And FC is equal to FB;

therefore the rectangle AE, EC together with the square on EF is equal to the square on FB.

For the same reason, also,

the rectangle DE, EB together with the square on FE is equal to the square on FB.

But the rectangle AE, EC together with the square on FE was also proved equal to the square on FB;

therefore the rectangle AE, EC together with the square on FE is equal to the rectangle DE, EB together with the square on FE.

Let the square on FE be subtracted from each;

therefore the rectangle contained by AE, EC which remains is equal to the rectangle contained by DE, EB.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

**How the Lean follows the text**

- **Done by `Prop35.cut`.** "Next let AC, DB not be through the centre…" Euclid's argument is written once for any straight line through E: it covers Simson's cases, where one straight line passes through the centre, and E at G, and serves for DB.

```lean
/-- This is Euclid's argument for one straight line AC through a point E other than the
centre F: the rectangle contained by AE, EC, together with the square on FE, is equal to the
square on FC. It serves as his "For the same reason" for DB, and covers the intermediate
cases, where one straight line passes through the centre or E is the foot of the
perpendicular. -/
theorem Prop35.cut {A C E F : Point} {α : Circle} (hF : Centre F α) (hA : OnCircle A α)
    (hC : OnCircle C α) (hAEC : Between A E C) (hEF : E ≠ F) :
    rect A E E C + sq F E = sq F C := by
  have hAC : A ≠ C := ne_of_between_ends hAEC
  obtain ⟨L, hA_L, hC_L⟩ := Postulate1 A C hAC
  have hE_L : OnLine E L := on_line_of_between_ends hAEC hA_L hC_L
  by_cases hF_AC : Collinear A C F
  · /- When AC passes through the centre, F bisects it, and II.5 applies there. -/
    obtain ⟨M, hA_M, hC_M, hF_M⟩ := hF_AC
    have hAFC : Between A F C :=
      between_of_inside_chord hF_M hA_M hC_M (centre_inside hF) hA hC hAC
    have hAF : ‖A F‖ = ‖F C‖ := by
      rw [len_symm A F]
      exact Definition15 hF hA hC
    exact BookII.Prop5 hAFC hAF hAEC hEF
  · /- The perpendicular from F, drawn by I.12, falls within AC (`foot_between`). -/
    obtain ⟨G, hG, hFG⟩ := BookI.Prop12 hAC hF_AC
    have hAGC : Between A G C := foot_between hF hA hC hF_AC hG hFG
    have hG_L : OnLine G L := on_line_of_between_ends hAGC hA_L hC_L
    have hF_L : ¬ OnLine F L := Triangle.off_line hF_AC hA_L hC_L
    have hFG' : F ≠ G := fun e => hF_L (e ▸ hG_L)
    have hAGF : ∠ A G F = ∟ := by
      rw [angle_symm (ne_of_between hAGC) hFG']
      exact hFG A ⟨L, hA_L, hC_L, hA_L⟩ (ne_of_between hAGC)
    /- It bisects AC [III. 3]. -/
    have hAG : ‖A G‖ = ‖G C‖ := (Prop3 hF hA hC hAGC hF_AC).2 hAGF
    /- AC is cut into equal parts at G and unequal parts at E [II. 5]; if E is G, the
       square on EG is nothing. -/
    have h5 : rect A E E C + sq E G = sq G C := by
      by_cases hEG : E = G
      · subst hEG
        rw [sq_self, add_zero]
        exact rect_congr hAG rfl
      · rw [sq_symm E G]
        exact BookII.Prop5 hAGC hAG hAEC hEG
    /- The square on GF is added to each. -/
    have hadd : rect A E E C + sq E G + sq G F = sq G C + sq G F :=
      CommonNotion2 h5 rfl
    /- The two right triangles replace the pairs of squares [I. 47]. -/
    have hFE : sq F E = sq E G + sq G F := by
      by_cases hEG : E = G
      · subst hEG
        rw [sq_self, add_comm, add_zero, sq_symm]
      · have t : Triangle G F E :=
          (Triangle.of_line hG_L hE_L (Ne.symm hEG) hF_L).acb
        rw [BookI.Prop47.sq t (hFG E ⟨L, hA_L, hC_L, hE_L⟩ hEG),
          sq_symm G E, sq_symm F G]
        ac_rfl
    have hFC : sq F C = sq G C + sq G F := by
      have hCG : C ≠ G := ne_of_between (between_symm hAGC)
      have t : Triangle G F C :=
        (Triangle.of_line hG_L hC_L (Ne.symm hCG) hF_L).acb
      rw [BookI.Prop47.sq t (hFG C ⟨L, hA_L, hC_L, hC_L⟩ hCG), sq_symm F G]
      ac_rfl
    rw [hFE, hFC, ← add_assoc]
    exact hadd
```

```lean
/-- If in a circle two straight lines cut one another, the rectangle contained by the segments of
the one is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments of the other. -/
theorem Prop35 {A B C D E : Point} {ABCD : Circle} (hABCD : ∃ F : Point, Centre F ABCD)
    (hA : OnCircle A ABCD) (hB : OnCircle B ABCD) (hC : OnCircle C ABCD)
    (hD : OnCircle D ABCD) (hAEC : Between A E C) (hBED : Between B E D) :
    rect A E E C = rect D E E B := by
  -- For in the circle ABCD let the two straight lines AC, BD cut one another at the point E;
  -- I say that the rectangle contained by AE, EC is equal to the rectangle contained by DE,
  -- EB.
  -- If now AC, BD are through the centre, so that E is the centre of the circle ABCD,
  by_cases hE : Centre E ABCD
  -- it is manifest that, AE, EC, DE, EB being equal,
  · have h₁ : ‖A E‖ = ‖D E‖ := by
      rw [len_symm A E, Definition15 hE hA hD, len_symm]
    have h₂ : ‖E C‖ = ‖E B‖ := Definition15 hE hC hB
    -- the rectangle contained by AE, EC is also equal to the rectangle contained by DE, EB.
    exact rect_congr h₁ h₂
  -- Next let AC, DB not be through the centre;
  -- let the centre of ABCD be taken, and let it be F;
  obtain ⟨F, -, -, -, hF, -⟩ := Prop1 hABCD hA hC (ne_of_between_ends hAEC)
  have hEF : E ≠ F := fun e => hE (e ▸ hF)
  have hAC : rect A E E C + sq F E = sq F C := by
    by_cases hF_AC : Collinear A C F
    · /- Robert Simson adds the intermediate cases, where AC passes through the centre
         and E does not. Then F bisects AC, and `Prop35.cut` gives the squares by II.5 at
         once. -/
      exact Prop35.cut hF hA hC hAEC hEF
    have hAC' : A ≠ C := ne_of_between_ends hAEC
    obtain ⟨L, hA_L, hC_L⟩ := Postulate1 A C hAC'
    have hE_L : OnLine E L := on_line_of_between_ends hAEC hA_L hC_L
    -- from F let FG, FH be drawn perpendicular to the straight lines AC, DB, and let FB, FC, FE
    -- be joined.
    obtain ⟨G, hG, hFG⟩ := BookI.Prop12 hAC' hF_AC
    /- FH is drawn in `Prop35.cut`, applied to DB below. The straight lines joined need
       no construction in Lean. -/
    -- Then, since a straight line GF through the centre cuts a straight line AC not through the
    -- centre at right angles,
    have hAGC : Between A G C := foot_between hF hA hC hF_AC hG hFG
    have hG_L : OnLine G L := on_line_of_between_ends hAGC hA_L hC_L
    have hF_L : ¬ OnLine F L := Triangle.off_line hF_AC hA_L hC_L
    have hFG' : F ≠ G := fun e => hF_L (e ▸ hG_L)
    have hAGF : ∠ A G F = ∟ := by
      rw [angle_symm (ne_of_between hAGC) hFG']
      exact hFG A ⟨L, hA_L, hC_L, hA_L⟩ (ne_of_between hAGC)
    -- it also bisects it; [III. 3]
    have hbisect := (Prop3 hF hA hC hAGC hF_AC).2 hAGF
    -- therefore AG is equal to GC.
    have hAG : ‖A G‖ = ‖G C‖ := hbisect
    -- Since, then, the straight line AC has been cut into equal parts at G and into unequal
    -- parts at E,
    -- the rectangle contained by AE, EC together with the square on EG is equal to the square on
    -- GC; [II. 5]
    have h5 : rect A E E C + sq E G = sq G C := by
      by_cases hEG : E = G
      · /- If E is G, the square on EG is nothing, as in `Prop35.cut`. -/
        subst hEG
        rw [sq_self, add_zero]
        exact rect_congr hAG rfl
      · rw [sq_symm E G]
        exact BookII.Prop5 hAGC hAG hAEC hEG
    -- Let the square on GF be added;
    have hadd := CommonNotion2 h5 (rfl : sq G F = sq G F)
    -- therefore the rectangle AE, EC together with the squares on GE, GF is equal to the squares
    -- on CG, GF.
    have hsum : rect A E E C + (sq G E + sq G F) = sq C G + sq G F := by
      rw [sq_symm G E, sq_symm C G, ← add_assoc]
      exact hadd
    -- But the square on FE is equal to the squares on EG, GF,
    have hFE : sq F E = sq E G + sq G F := by
      by_cases hEG : E = G
      · subst hEG
        rw [sq_self, add_comm, add_zero, sq_symm]
      · have t : Triangle G F E :=
          (Triangle.of_line hG_L hE_L (Ne.symm hEG) hF_L).acb
        rw [BookI.Prop47.sq t (hFG E ⟨L, hA_L, hC_L, hE_L⟩ hEG),
          sq_symm G E, sq_symm F G]
        ac_rfl
    -- and the square on FC is equal to the squares on CG, GF; [I. 47]
    have hFC : sq F C = sq C G + sq G F := by
      have hCG : C ≠ G := ne_of_between (between_symm hAGC)
      have t : Triangle G F C :=
        (Triangle.of_line hG_L hC_L (Ne.symm hCG) hF_L).acb
      rw [BookI.Prop47.sq t (hFG C ⟨L, hA_L, hC_L, hC_L⟩ hCG),
        sq_symm F G, sq_symm G C]
      ac_rfl
    -- therefore the rectangle AE, EC together with the square on FE is equal to the square on
    -- FC.
    rw [hFE, hFC, sq_symm E G]
    exact hsum
  -- And FC is equal to FB;
  have hFC_FB : ‖F C‖ = ‖F B‖ := Definition15 hF hC hB
  -- therefore the rectangle AE, EC together with the square on EF is equal to the square on
  -- FB.
  rw [sq_congr hFC_FB] at hAC
  -- For the same reason, also,
  -- the rectangle DE, EB together with the square on FE is equal to the square on FB.
  have hDB : rect D E E B + sq F E = sq F B :=
    Prop35.cut hF hD hB (between_symm hBED) hEF
  -- But the rectangle AE, EC together with the square on FE was also proved equal to the
  -- square on FB;
  -- therefore the rectangle AE, EC together with the square on FE is equal to the rectangle
  -- DE, EB together with the square on FE.
  have hboth : rect A E E C + sq F E = rect D E E B + sq F E := hAC.trans hDB.symm
  -- Let the square on FE be subtracted from each;
  -- therefore the rectangle contained by AE, EC which remains is equal to the rectangle
  -- contained by DE, EB.
  exact CommonNotion3 hboth rfl
  -- Therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.
```

- [`between_of_between_left`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L66): If B is between A and C, and D is between A and B, then D is between A and C. (Between 4)
- [`between_of_between_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L70) (through [`BookI.Prop47.sq`](../../Elements/BookII/Rectangles.lean#L380)): If B is between A and C, and C is between B and D, then B is between A and D. (Between 5)
- [`between_of_inside_chord`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L155) (used here): A straight line through a point inside a circle has that point between the points where it meets the circle. (Circle 1)
- [`between_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L43) (used here): If B is between A and C, it is between C and A. (Between 1)
- [`centre_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L35) (used here): The centre of a circle is inside it. (Generalities 3)
- [`circles_meet`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L201): If each circle passes through a point inside the other, the circles cut one another. This is the step Euclid takes for granted in I.1. (Intersection 5)

- [`same_side_trans`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L96) (through [`BookI.Prop47.sq`](../../Elements/BookII/Rectangles.lean#L380)): Two points on the same side of a straight line as a third point are on the same side as each other. (Same side 4)
- [`triple_incidence1`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L131) (through [`BookI.Prop47.sq`](../../Elements/BookII/Rectangles.lean#L380)): Take B on L, C on M and D on N, three straight lines through A. If C lies within the angle BAD (on D's side of L and on B's side of N), then B and D are not on the same side of M: the straight line AC separates them. (Triple incidence 1)
- [`triple_incidence2`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L139): Take B on L, C on M and D on N, three straight lines through A, with B other than A and D off M. If C and D are on the same side of L, and B and D are not on the same side of M, then B and C are on the same side of N: C lies within the angle BAD. (Triple incidence 2)

**Lengths, angles and areas**

- [`adjacent_eq_of_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L67): A right angle is equal to the angle adjacent to it. (Diagram-angle 3; the other half is Definition 10 together with Postulate 4)
- [`angle_add_of_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L54): If D lies within the angle BAC, then BAC is made up of BAD and DAC. (Diagram-angle 2)
- [`angle_eq_of_same_rays`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L72): The angle doesn't change if its arms are traced through other points on the same rays. (Diagram-angle 4)
- [`angle_le_two_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L29): No angle exceeds two right angles. (Metric 5)
- [`angle_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L26) (used here): The angle ABC is the angle CBA. (Metric 4)
- [`area_add_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L88) (through [`BookI.Prop47.sq`](../../Elements/BookII/Rectangles.lean#L380)): Cutting a triangle in two from a vertex adds up. (Diagram-area 2)
- [`area_congruent`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L43): Triangles equal in all their sides and angles are equal in area. Euclid uses this without comment once he has shown two triangles congruent. (Metric 9)
- [`area_degenerate`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L32) (through [`BookI.Prop47.sq`](../../Elements/BookII/Rectangles.lean#L380)): A "triangle" with a repeated corner has no area. (Metric 6)
- [`area_eq_zero_of_on_line`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L80) (through [`BookI.Prop47.sq`](../../Elements/BookII/Rectangles.lean#L380)): A "triangle" whose corners lie on one straight line has no area. (Diagram-area 1)
- [`area_rotate`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L35) (through [`BookI.Prop47.sq`](../../Elements/BookII/Rectangles.lean#L380)): The triangle ABC is the triangle CAB. (Metric 8)
- [`area_swap`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L38) (through [`BookI.Prop47.sq`](../../Elements/BookII/Rectangles.lean#L380)): The triangle ABC is the triangle ACB. (Metric 8)
- [`eq_of_len_eq_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L17) (through [`BookI.Prop47.sq`](../../Elements/BookII/Rectangles.lean#L380) and [`sq_self`](../../Elements/Figure/Rectangles.lean#L128)): A finite straight line with distinct ends has length. (Metric 1)
- [`inside_of_len_lt`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L33) (through [`foot_between`](../../Elements/BookIII/Squares.lean#L95)): A point nearer the centre than the circumference is inside. (Diagram-segment 4)
- [`len_add_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L21): If B is between A and C, then AB and BC together make up AC. (Diagram-segment 1)
- [`len_lt_of_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L37): A point inside is nearer the centre than the circumference. (Diagram-segment 4)
- [`len_self`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L20) (through [`sq_self`](../../Elements/Figure/Rectangles.lean#L128)): The "straight line" from a point to itself has no length. (Metric 1)
- [`len_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L23) (used here): The straight line AB is the straight line BA. (Metric 3)
- [`on_line_of_area_eq_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L84): A triangle with no area has its corners on one straight line. (Diagram-area 1)
- [`same_ray_of_angle_eq_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L49): If the angle BAC is nothing, C lies on the ray from A through B. (Diagram-angle 1)

**Superposition**

- [`superposition`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Superposition.lean#L30): **Superposition.** The triangle ABC can be applied to the straight line L with A on D, B on the ray from D through G, and C on the side of L where H is, without changing any side or angle.

**Laws of magnitude**

- [`add_assoc`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L23) (used here): Adding three magnitudes in a row, it makes no difference whether the first two or the last two are added first. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_comm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L26) (used here): The order of adding does not matter. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_lt_add_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L45) (through [`foot_between`](../../Elements/BookIII/Squares.lean#L95)): Adding the same thing to both sides keeps "less than". (System E §3.5)
- [`add_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L29) (used here): Adding nothing changes nothing. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_irrefl`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L32) (through [`foot_between`](../../Elements/BookIII/Squares.lean#L95)): No magnitude is less than itself. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trans`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L35) (through [`foot_between`](../../Elements/BookIII/Squares.lean#L95)): What is less than the less is less still. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trichotomy`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L39) (through [`foot_between`](../../Elements/BookIII/Squares.lean#L95)): Of two magnitudes, one is less, or they are equal, or the other is less. (System E §3.5)
- [`not_lt_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L42): Nothing is less than zero. (System E §3.5)

</details>

## Mishnah

_Our commentary: what Euclid assumes, what Lean made us say out loud, and how the result looks by modern means._

**The square on FE, added and taken away.** When E is the centre, AE, EC, DE and EB are radii, and Euclid calls the equality manifest. Otherwise he adds the square on FE to each rectangle and finds the square on a radius both times; take the square on FE away again, and the rectangles are equal. Everything rests on one fact about the isosceles triangle FAC: the rectangle AE, EC together with the square on FE is equal to the square on FC. Isaac Todhunter remarked that much of the proofs of III.35 and III.36 amounts to this fact, and Heath adds that it follows at once from I.47 with II.5 or II.6 (vol. 2, p. 73).

**Must every case be drawn?** Robert Simson, following Johannes Campanus, adds the cases where one straight line passes through the centre and the other does not; he thought Theon, or some other editor, had left them out as too long. Heath disagrees: "in giving the simplest and most difficult cases only, he seems to be following quite consistently his habit of avoiding *too great* multiplicity of cases, while not ignoring their existence" (vol. 2, p. 73). So Euclid draws the easiest figure and the hardest, and trusts us with the rest.

**What if E is G?** Then AC is cut equally at E, and II.5, which needs an unequal cut, has nothing to give. But the square on EG is then nothing, and the rectangle AE, EC is already the square on GC, so the argument holds all the same. Lean has no figure to choose from, so we take Simson's cases too. Euclid's argument, written for any straight line through E (`Prop35.cut`), covers a straight line through the centre and this case, and serves for DB as Euclid's "For the same reason".

**The modern way.** This is the power of a point: for a circle of centre F and radius r, the power of a point E is FE² − r², negative inside the circle, and AE · EC = DE · EB = r² − FE² is that power with its sign changed.

## Further reading

- For the power of a point given a sign, as in the modern way, "the product of its oriented distances to any two points of the circle collinear with it", Julian Lowell Coolidge's [*A Treatise on the Circle and the Sphere*](https://archive.org/details/cu31924001508955) (1916, free online), ch. I, §2, "Inversion" (p. 30) (also on [III.21](21.md)).
- For III.35 and III.36 drawn as one "basic theorem", with the remark that "The Greek geometers took great pains to enumerate the different 'cases' of each theorem. Today we prefer, when possible, to treat all variants together in one compact theorem", C. Stanley Ogilvy's [*Excursions in Geometry*](https://store.doverpublications.com/products/9780486265308) (1969), ch. 1, "A basic theorem" (pp. 8–9) (also on [III.19](19.md)).
- For the cases Simson put back "from the translation from the Arabic", believing that Theon, or some other, "has thought them too long to insert", Robert Simson's [*The Elements of Euclid*](https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_elements-english-sele_euclid_1756_0) (1756, free online), his note on III.35 (p. 368) (also on [III.1](01.md)).
